# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy resulting from the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered rare and untreatable, CA is now increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, and arrhythmia [1,2]. Advances in noninvasive imaging and the advent of disease-modifying therapies have transformed the clinical landscape, making early diagnosis imperative [3].

## Pathophysiology and Classification

More than 30 precursor proteins can form amyloid, but two types account for the overwhelming majority of cardiac involvement: immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [4]. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia produces misfolded light chains that are directly cardiotoxic in addition to causing fibrillar deposition [5]. ATTR amyloidosis arises from the destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer, a hepatically synthesized transport protein for thyroxine and retinol [6]. ATTR is subclassified into a hereditary form (ATTRv), caused by pathogenic *TTR* variants such as Val122Ile and Val30Met, and a wild-type form (ATTRwt), historically termed senile systemic amyloidosis, which predominantly affects elderly men [7,8].

## Epidemiology

The true prevalence of CA has been underestimated. Autopsy and imaging studies suggest that ATTRwt is present in up to 13–25% of elderly patients with HFpEF and in a substantial fraction of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement [9,10]. The Val122Ile *TTR* variant is carried by approximately 3–4% of individuals of West African ancestry, contributing to disparities in heart failure outcomes [11].

## Clinical Presentation

Cardiac involvement manifests as progressive heart failure, often with preserved ejection fraction but markedly impaired diastolic function [12]. Extracardiac red flags aid recognition: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture frequently precede the cardiac diagnosis in ATTR [13]. Conduction disease, atrial fibrillation, and low QRS voltages relative to wall thickness on electrocardiography are characteristic findings [14]. AL amyloidosis may additionally present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, periorbital purpura, and macroglossia [5].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically reveals increased ventricular wall thickness, a granular sparkling myocardial texture, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic apical-sparing pattern of longitudinal strain ("cherry-on-top") [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [16]. A major diagnostic advance has been bone scintigraphy with technetium-labeled tracers (e.g., ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD or ⁹⁹ᵐTc-PYP), which shows avid myocardial uptake in ATTR amyloidosis [17]. A landmark validation study demonstrated that grade 2–3 cardiac uptake, in the absence of a monoclonal protein, has a specificity and positive predictive value approaching 100% for ATTR-CA, permitting noninvasive diagnosis [18]. Critically, monoclonal protein must be excluded with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assays before relying on scintigraphy, since AL amyloidosis can also produce cardiac tracer uptake [19]. Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry-based typing remains the gold standard when results are equivocal [20].

## Prognosis and Staging

Untreated AL-CA carries a particularly grim prognosis, with median survival of only months in advanced disease. Staging systems incorporating cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), refined by the difference in free light chains, stratify risk in AL [21]. Analogous ATTR staging systems use NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate [22].

## Treatment

Management of AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma cell clone. The addition of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone significantly improved hematologic and cardiac responses in the ANDROMEDA trial [23]. For ATTR-CA, the transthyretin stabilizer tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial, becoming the first approved therapy [24]. Gene-silencing agents, including the small interfering RNA patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, were first validated in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [25,26], and patisiran has subsequently been studied in cardiomyopathy [27]. More recently, novel agents such as the stabilizer acoramidis and the next-generation silencer vutrisiran have demonstrated favorable cardiovascular outcomes [28,29]. CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing has shown durable reductions in serum transthyretin, offering the prospect of a one-time treatment [30].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from a diagnostic curiosity to a treatable condition. Heightened clinical suspicion, judicious use of noninvasive imaging, and rigorous exclusion of a monoclonal protein enable timely diagnosis, while an expanding therapeutic armamentarium now offers meaningful improvements in survival and quality of life.
